Record, train, and deploy from one place with Strands Agents, LeRobot, and Hugging Face Storage Buckets

📅 13 Aug 2026 | ⏱️ 16 min read (3224 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hugging Face

⏱️ ~16 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • A walkthrough of the streaming data loop in Strands Robots, one loop that records robot demonstrations, trains on them by reading straight from the Hub, and deploys the policy back to hardware, with the dataset in the same on-disk LeRobot format the whole way through.
  • It has been revealed that you have an agent that can already drive a robot while your code records a demonstration and pushes it to the Hugging Face Hub.
  • The first post in this series introduced Strands Robots, an open source SDK from AWS (Apache 2.0) that exposes robot abstractions, simulation, and the LeRobot stack as AgentTools you compose into a single Strands agent.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A walkthrough of the streaming data loop in Strands Robots, one loop that records robot demonstrations, trains on them by reading straight from the Hub, and deploys the policy back to hardware, with the dataset in the same on-disk LeRobot format the whole way through.

Updated for Strands Robots 0.6 and LeRobot 0.7.

It has been revealed that you have an agent that can already drive a robot while your code records a demonstration and pushes it to the Hugging Face Hub. Now you want to run that loop continuously: collect episodes through the day, train a policy on the growing dataset, deploy it, and pull the next batch back to improve it. Run that loop once and every piece works. Run it every day and you start paying for the same byte transfers over and over. The recordings you upload keep growing, each training run copies the whole dataset to the GPUs before it starts, and every fresh checkpoint ships out while the next batch of recordings comes back.

The first post in this series introduced Strands Robots, an open source SDK from AWS (Apache 2.0) that exposes robot abstractions, simulation, and the LeRobot stack as AgentTools you compose into a single Strands agent. That post followed the agent loop in one direction, from a Hub dataset to a physical robot. This one follows the data the other way, from the first recorded frame back to the deployed policy, over Hugging Face Storage Buckets - a mutable, non-versioned, Xet-backed object-storage repository type announced in March 2026. A bucket sits beside your dataset repositories in the same hf:// namespace and uses the hf CLI you already have, so it becomes the working layer that holds your data between the day you record it and the day you train on it.

Someone has to decide which episodes to keep, when the scene has drifted far enough to re-record, whether today's batch is enough to train on, and which checkpoint replaces the one on the arm. Each of those decisions comes up dozens of times over a collection campaign, and each one needs a look at what came back before the next command goes out. That is the work an agent is for: it drives the robot and reads the results, while the recording itself stays one line of your code. This post walks you through the data loop: record a demonstration into a Storage Bucket, store it so that each sync uploads only the bytes that changed, train by streaming the dataset straight from the Hub instead of downloading it, and deploy the checkpoint back to hardware with one keyword argument change. The runnable companion to this post lives at notebooks/12_streaming_data_loop.ipynb.

It has been revealed that where the first post recorded a dataset and pushed it to the Hub, the loop you build here records a LeRobotDataset with one run(record=...) call, syncs it into a Storage Bucket, and streams that same dataset back frame by frame, decoding camera video on the fly, with no local copy. You read it back with LeRobot's own streaming reader, so the dataset Robot() recorded is exactly the one LeRobot trains on. Your trained checkpoint then deploys to that same Robot() with one keyword argument change, and the demonstrations it records on hardware return to the same bucket.

Industry observers note that figure 1. The four stages share one backend. Robot("so101") records a LeRobotDataset with run(record=...); hf sync syncs it into a Storage Bucket; lerobot-train reads it back over the Hub through LeRobot's StreamingLeRobotDataset with no full download; and the trained checkpoint deploys to the same Robot with a port=. The on-disk format stays exactly as LeRobot wrote it.

Recent findings suggest that when the agent runs an episode, it invokes one tool, and the rollout then proceeds at the robot's control frequency until the episode ends, with the policy producing every action. Stripped down to the code, the whole loop is a handful of lines:.

What follows is what's actually happening inside that loop, step by step.

That's it. Every stage in this post runs on a laptop with these three, plus the bucket and training items under Advanced. What runs is the loop, not a working policy: the default path uses a placeholder wave function, which records a valid dataset but not a useful one.

You record upcoming episodes through the day, each a continuous run of camera frames and joint state-action telemetry. LeRobot writes that as a small set of large files that grow as you record. Push them into a versioned dataset repository and every append becomes a commit, and every revision is retained. Collection wants the reverse: somewhere to write bytes and overwrite them in place. That is a Storage Bucket, which lives inside your Hugging Face workspace and uses the permissions you already have. There are no identity and access management (IAM) roles to configure, no cross-origin resource sharing (CORS) rules, and no upload service to maintain.

In a recent development, strands Robots records a LeRobotDataset in the same format LeRobot writes on hardware: pass record= to run(), and each run adds one episode. Record the episodes, then sync the finished dataset into a bucket. The wave function is a placeholder that produces joint targets without a trained model, so you can run the whole loop before you have a checkpoint to run:.

The sync writes to hf://buckets/{bucket}/{run_id}, where run_id is the folder name that follows the bucket, cube_pick here. The streaming read in Step 3 names the run too: the first two segments of the id are the bucket, and everything after them is the path inside it.

In a recent development, each sync uploads only the files that changed. Write to the bucket through the day, and publish a versioned copy to a dataset repository when you want one: record="hf://my_user/cube_picking", push=True does that at the end of a run. The placeholder episodes are not useful training data. Pass a trained Policy("") to run() instead.

To record on a physical SO-101, LeRobot's record CLI handles the leader-follower bring-up:.

The dataset lands on disk in the same format as the simulation recording, so the same sync takes it to a bucket: hf sync ~/.cache/huggingface/lerobot/my_user/cube_picking hf://buckets/my-org/robot-fave/run-021. Collection runs append into one place, and your published repositories only get the versions you choose to publish.

Now that a dataset is in the bucket, the question is what the next sync costs you. Point two fixed cameras at an arm clearing the same table for eight hours and most of what you record is pixels you already have: the same lighting, the same chassis, the same background, across thousands of episodes. On a versioned repository it gets worse, because changing one frame in a multi-gigabyte video shard re-uploads the whole file.

Buckets are backed by Xet, which deduplicates your uploads at the byte level using content-defined chunking. Chunk boundaries follow the content, so inserting a few bytes changes only the chunk it lands in instead of shifting every boundary after it. In Hugging Face's own measurements (HF Storage), content-defined chunking reduces data transferred per upload by about four times across the Hub, and on Enterprise looks billing is on the deduplicated footprint. Their bucket benchmarks show what that looks like on a single file. Starting from a 500 MB upload, changing 1% of the bytes and re-uploading moved 5.5 MB, changing 5% moved 27.5 MB, and changing 10% moved 55 MB. Without chunk-level deduplication, overwriting an object means sending all of its bytes again, whether or not they changed.

How much that saves you depends on the file layout, and the Strands Robots recorder uses LeRobot's. Episodes go into Parquet shards (data/chunk-000/file-000.parquet) and per-camera MP4 shards (videos/observation.images.front/chunk-000/file-000.mp4), rolling to a latest file when the current one fills, at LeRobot's defaults of 100 MB for data Parquet and 200 MB for video MP4. Each run(record=...) starts its own shards, and a lerobot-record session grows its open shard until it fills. Either way, a sync after a day of recording uploads the new trailing shards plus, at most, the one partially-filled shard that grew, rather than the whole dataset. Sync the same bucket again tomorrow and Xet handles the deduplication.

Recent findings suggest that figure 2. A sync uploads only what changed. The first sync of a fresh dataset uploads every chunk; after recording more episodes, Xet's content-defined chunking means the next sync uploads only the newly introduced chunks and skips the ones already stored.

In a recent development, to train, you point GPUs at your dataset. Download it first and those GPUs sit idle until hundreds of gigabytes finish copying. Streaming straight from the Hub works here because of the shard layout from Step 2: a batch becomes a few byte-range reads over large shards rather than thousands of small fetches. LeRobot's StreamingLeRobotDataset turns that into a drop-in torch iterable, and it opens a bucket with repo_type="bucket":.

Figure 3. Stream, don't download. The download path copies the whole dataset to local disk first, so the GPU waits; StreamingLeRobotDataset reads batches straight from the bucket with only metadata on local disk, so the GPU trains from the first batch.

It has been revealed that nothing lands on local disk except the small meta/ folder of schema, statistics, and episode index, plus a seek index for the video shards: a full streaming read of the 86 MB lerobot/svla_so101_pickplace dataset left under 1 MB on disk. Camera frames are decoded from the remote MP4 shards as you iterate; state and action come from the Parquet shards. That loop reads one frame at a time, which suits inspecting an episode. To train, pass the reader to a DataLoader and iterate batches instead. The streaming dataset shuffles internally through a bounded reservoir buffer, so video decoding parallelizes across worker processes:.

On macOS, run that from a script with an if __name__ == "__main__": guard, because DataLoader workers start by re-importing the script.

It has been revealed that if you would rather not write the loop at all, LeRobot's own trainer reads through the same engine, so the dataset you collected trains without a line of new code. It takes a bucket through the same keyword argument the in-process reader uses:.

Sources indicate that buckets are streaming-only, so --dataset.repo_type=bucket requires --dataset.streaming=true and the config rejects the combination otherwise. --policy.push_to_hub=false keeps the checkpoint local; name a --policy.repo_id to publish it instead. Reach for StreamingLeRobotDataset directly when you want the loop in your own process: validating an episode, replaying it in simulation, or feeding a custom evaluation loop.

The checkpoint lerobot-train writes loads straight back through the same entry point used to run any other policy, so the record-train-deploy loop closes in a few lines:.

A 20-step CPU run of ACT over the two-episode dataset above, streamed from a private bucket, wrote a checkpoint that Policy() loaded and ran on the simulated arm. Twenty steps over placeholder episodes check that the loop connects; it does not train a policy that grasps. Training time scales with dataset size, batch size, and step count, and a useful ACT policy needs real demonstrations and a GPU.

Sources indicate that hugging Face's pre-warming caches bucket data at edge locations near the cloud and region where your jobs run, so your cluster reads locally and the dataloader stays ahead of the GPU. In Hugging Face's own bucket benchmarks, a warm content delivery network (CDN) read hit about 1,086 MB/s on a 10 GB payload against 780 MB/s cold, and roughly 1,124 MB/s warm at 100 GB, measured on an m5dn.24xlarge in us-east-1. The full comparison against plain object storage, upload as well as download, is on that dashboard. Choosing where that data lives is a Storage Regions setting on Team and Enterprise intends, as of this writing US and EU, with Asia-Pacific and Gulf Cooperation Council (GCC) regions unveiled as coming; outside those plans repositories are stored in the US.

In a recent development, in this step you take the checkpoint you just trained, run it on a physical robot, and record the next round of demonstrations with it. This is the same agent code from the first post. The keyword argument that changes is port=, which selects the physical arm; id= names its LeRobot calibration, cameras= names the image keys the policy was trained on, and operator= approves its moves.

According to recent reports, nothing moves on the real arm until operator= approves it. The demonstrations it records with record= are in the same LeRobot format you started with, ready to sync back to the bucket for the next training run.

In a recent development, if your data already lives on Amazon Simple Storage Service (Amazon S3), nothing in this post changes: a LeRobotDataset is a directory of Parquet and MP4 shards, and every step reads it wherever it sits. A bucket adds the Hub-native path, the sync and the streaming read, with no storage to provision first.

Run the loop again tomorrow and you record into the same bucket, sync only what changed, and stream it to the GPUs without waiting for a download. The data never leaves the LeRobot format.

Industry observers note that the full Strands Robots sample is on GitHub at strands-labs/robots in notebooks/12_streaming_data_loop.ipynb. It walks you through the full loop cell by cell: record, sync to a bucket, stream back, train, and load the checkpoint. Every cell runs in simulation on the placeholder policy, so no GPU and no Docker are needed, and without a bucket set it needs no Hugging Face credentials either.

Run the cells top to bottom. To sync to a bucket, set HF_BUCKET=my-org/robot-fave before starting Jupyter (after hf auth login); each run syncs under its own folder, nb12-, and the notebook streams back from it. Without HF_BUCKET it trains from the local folder instead. To train on a GPU, raise --steps and drop --policy.device=cpu in the training cell.

Recent findings suggest that the snippets here are a "hello world" of the Strands Robots data loop. Five things change once you run it against real data.

Sources indicate that prompt injection. Supplying untrusted data to an agent can lead to prompt injection, where untrustworthy context is treated as LLM instructions. These agents actuate robots, so this is an important risk to track. Feed the agent only data from trusted sources. If not all input can be trusted, restrict the tools available to the agent so it cannot take safety-critical actions. In Strands Robots an agent cannot record, push, or calibrate, and on a real robot operator= answers every move and every policy run's blueprint before anything moves.

Training data is a trust boundary. Anything that can write into the collection bucket can also write episodes that a policy later trains on, and that policy drives a physical arm. Keep the credential that writes collection data separate from the one a training job reads with, sync each run under its own run_id so an episode can be traced to the run that produced it and removed on its own, and treat the versioned dataset repository as the reviewed artifact, because the bucket keeps no revisions to audit against.

Sources indicate that bucket credentials and scope. hf sync and StreamingLeRobotDataset use the token from hf auth login. Use a token scoped to the specific namespace you are writing to, prefer --private buckets for collection data, and keep the bucket distinct from the versioned dataset repository you publish and share.

Overwrite in place keeps no revisions. A bucket overwrites in place and retains no revisions, which is what makes it a working layer and also means a repeated run_id replaces the run already stored there. Sync each collection run to its own path, as in hf sync ./recordings hf://buckets/my-org/robot-fave/run-021. For anything you need to be able to return to, push to a versioned dataset repository, where every revision is retained.

Recent findings suggest that only use trusted Hugging Face orgs. Loading a checkpoint runs code its publisher chose. A Policy your own code builds loads directly; a Hub checkpoint the agent asks for by name loads only if the operator lists it in STRANDS_POLICY_REPOS (for example STRANDS_POLICY_REPOS=lerobot/smolvla_base,my_user/*). Only load checkpoints from organizations you trust. Model weights can contain arbitrary code (pickle-based checkpoints). Prefer safetensors-format checkpoints where available.

Sources indicate that the loop leaves a bucket, datasets under /tmp, and a checkpoint on disk. Bucket contents count toward your stored volume, so remove what you no longer need:.

Stop any training process still on a GPU instance, and stop the instance. If you ran the notebook, its last cell prints the command that removes its run. Anything you published to a dataset repository is versioned and is untouched.

Recent findings suggest that the Strands Robots documentation covers the robot catalog, simulation, policies, recording, and the mesh in depth. The recording guide documents run(record=...) and reading a dataset back with LeRobot.

If you collect from more than one robot, give each one its own run_id and they write into the same bucket in parallel. The multi-robot mesh fans one agent out across those robots, so the same loop becomes a fleet collecting through the day into shared storage. A streaming reader reads one run at a time, so point each training run at the run_id it should learn from.

If you want a larger policy than ACT, lerobot-train fine-tunes LeRobot's vision-language-action (VLA) policies, such as SmolVLA and pi0, on the dataset you just streamed, and the checkpoint loads as a Policy the same way. For heavier simulation to generate that data, the Newton (newton) and Isaac Sim (isaac) backends sit behind the same Robot(), so the agent code does not change as you scale up.

Recent findings suggest that bucket streaming reached LeRobot through contributions from both the Strands Robots and LeRobot teams, upstream in LeRobot itself, so the datasets your agent collects are readable by every tool in that ecosystem. That runs both ways: the reader in Step 3 opens any of the LeRobot datasets already published on the Hub, so you can replay and evaluate against existing demonstrations before you record any of your own.

Sources indicate that contributions are welcome under Apache 2.0. If you build something with this loop, open an problem with what worked and what didn't.

Recent findings suggest that what makes this architecture particularly compelling is that the agent isn’t just executing a task—it’s sitting inside a continuous data, learning, and deployment loop. Connecting data collection, streaming, training, evaluation, and deployment through one agent workflow opens up some fascinating possibilities for adaptive systems. At the same time, the trust boundaries around data, credentials, and agent actions become critical. This is where custom AI agent development and enterprise AI agent solutions need to be designed as complete systems rather than isolated agent features. I came across Mobisoft Infotech while exploring this space: https://mobisoftinfotech.com/services/ai-agent-development-organization.

According to recent reports, arXiv:2611.21784v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Studies of how long code from AI coding agents survives after it is merged reach conflicting verdicts: agent code is reported to be retained longer than human code, about as long, or modified sooner. Each study makes defensible measurement choices, but how much these choices decide the verdict is unknown. We revisit the survival of agent-attributed code in our earlier study: 854,139 lines that 2,802 merged pull requests (PRs) added to 215 repositories of the AIDev dataset. We vary nine measurement choices in five research questions and build a specification curve of 88 survival analyses, tested under three variance estimators, several observation windows, and permuted labels. For code from human-supervised agents, mostly GitHub Copilot, the choices change the size of the effect but not its direction. For code from the fully-autonomous agent Devin, they decide the verdict. Across repositories, 15 of 22 specifications report it modified sooner when lines are treated as independent, but only 3 when standard errors are clustered by repository, no more than permuted labels produce. Within repositories, no specification detects a difference. LLM intent classifiers agree with human labels about as well as two humans agree with each other, whereas keyword rules do not (kappa = 0.69 to 0.72 against 0.38), and the two reach different verdicts on why agent code is modified. Humans make most modifications to agent code under every unit and window. Re-run on our data, five published designs each change their result with a single choice. Whether agent code survives longer than human code is therefore decided as much by the measurement as by the code. We derive an operationalization checklist for post-merge studies.

📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 1 min read (258 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Arxiv

Sources indicate that arXiv:2611.21781v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Deep-learning methods have achieved strong performance in EEG artifact removal, but evaluation remains dominated by reconstruction metrics such as error, correlation, and signal-to-noise ratio. Although these metrics assess similarity to clean EEG, they do not establish whether models effectively suppress artifacts, preserve neural activity, or provide reliable explanations. To address these limitations, we propose TriX-EEG, a three-level framework for trustworthy and explainable EEG artifact removal. Level 1, Signal Validity (SV), evaluates reconstruction quality and neural band-power preservation. Level 2, Removal Faithfulness (RF), assesses the removed component through artifact error and residual artifact/neural leakage. Level 3, Explanation Reliability (ER), examines model behavior through temporal alignment, causal relevance, and stability. We evaluate TriX-EEG using nine published neural denoisers across three public benchmarks derived from EEGDenoiseNet and the PhysioNet Motion Artifact Contaminated EEG Dataset, covering EOG, EMG, and motion artifacts. Results show that reconstruction metrics alone are insufficient for trustworthy denoiser assessment: RF complements it by revealing whether errors stem from residual artifact or suppressed neural activity, while ER captures distinct aspects of explanation behavior, supporting joint evaluation of three aspects within a unified framework rather than reliance on any single factor. External validation on an independent EEG/EOG dataset and the BCI Competition IV-2a motor-imagery dataset further demonstrates broadly consistent rankings under dataset shift. Higher-ranked denoisers generally preserve more task-relevant information or cause less downstream performance degradation. Overall, TriX-EEG provides a comprehensive basis for EEG denoiser assessment, encouraging models that are not only accurate but also faithful and explainable.

#3598. State of Open Models: Summer 2026 Observations

📅 14 Aug 2026 • ⏱️ 14m • 📚 Deep Dive (2754 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Hugging Face ↗ Open Full Page

State of Open Models: Summer 2026 Observations

📅 14 Aug 2026 | ⏱️ 14 min read (2754 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hugging Face

⏱️ ~14 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In the AI world, time feels compressed.
  • Models and datasets on HF hub are growing on a daily basis.
  • Industry observers note that there used to be a clear progression path: labs would start by releasing smaller models and gradually work their way toward the top end of the scale.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In the AI world, time feels compressed. A few months after our spring report in our biannual analysis worked through the ecosystem, there are quite a few findings that we have observed until this summer. This report lays out these observations from January to August 2026 and presents the data behind each one.

Models and datasets on HF hub are growing on a daily basis. Public model repositories grew from 2.43 to 2.96 million over the period, datasets from 711,000 to 1 million, Spaces from 1.00 to 1.44 million. The distribution underneath stays extreme, roughly 85.6% of models have fewer than 200 lifetime downloads, and 1.5% of repositories account for 99.2% of all downloads. Everything below happens inside that shape.

Industry observers note that there used to be a clear progression path: labs would start by releasing smaller models and gradually work their way toward the top end of the scale. In 2026, several Chinese labs skipped this progression entirely.

Industry observers note that in almost every month of 2026, the largest and most performant open model from a Chinese lab was larger than any model an American lab released. China's monthly ceiling ran between 754B and 2.78 trillion parameters; U.S. models stayed under 130B in five of seven months, the exception being NVIDIA's Nemotron 3 Ultra at 561B in May and June, and Inkling from Thinking Machines Lab.

Sources indicate that the chart splits the labs into two camps. Moonshot, MiniMax, Xiaomi and Z.ai publish almost nothing below 70B, so a developer's first encounter with them is a model too large to run on anything they own. Tencent and Alibaba Qwen cover the whole range instead, from under 1B upward.

Two things made the first camp possible. Building large stopped being a differentiator. Xiaomi, Ant Group and Meituan all cleared a trillion parameters this year, and neither was a household name in open weights twelve months ago. And a lab no longer has to ship a small model to be reachable, because the community's quantization layer will make a large one runnable within days, a dependency we return to below.

Recent findings suggest that that leaves the size profile as a statement of intent rather than of capability. A frontier only portfolio stakes everything on benchmark position and API demand. A full spectrum portfolio is a bid to be the family developers standardise on. Both are rational, they are playing for different prizes.

The United States is not absent from open source.

The two organizations publishing the most latest open models this year are also the companies making the hardware: AMD and NVIDIA. Each released more than 200 new model repositories, far ahead of the rest of the field, with LiquidAI ranking third at around 100. Hardware vendors have realized that open models are a way to sell chips: a model optimized for your hardware and freely available is the clearest proof that the hardware works.

When smaller models and embedding models are included, where Google, Microsoft, IBM Granite, and OpenAI’s older vision and speech models generate hundreds of millions of downloads annually, U.S. open source AI is growing.

More hardware and infrastructure organizations such as NVIDIA are training and open-weighting competitive models. NVIDIA's Nemotron model family boasts high performance. Long-time leaders such as Meta reignite open roots with Meta's Muse Glimmer.

According to recent reports, at the frontier scale, some U.S. model releases above 100B parameters this year are built on top of Chinese models or leverage artifacts from Chinese labs, such as Thinking Machines’ Inkling (952B). Major original American models include NVIDIA’s Nemotron 3 Ultra (561B), Nemotron 3 Super (124B), and Arcee AI’s Trinity-Large (399B).

AMD contributed many conversions. This work is notable: it enables trillion-parameter models to run efficiently on U.S. hardware. This represents a distribution and optimization layer.

Meanwhile, Chinese open models are increasingly optimized for domestic chips in China, the same competition in reverse, where models are designed around specific hardware ecosystems.

We took the top 25 model repositories by downloads accumulated this year and the top 25 by likes. Exactly one repository appears in both lists.

Industry observers note that we counted downloads inside the window rather than lifetime, so nothing is credited for merely having existed longer, and controlling for age makes the split sharper. Not one model published in 2026 reaches the download top 25, while thirteen of the twenty-five date from 2022. all-MiniLM-L6-v2 was pulled 1.55 billion times in seven months against 5,156 likes; Kimi-K3 was pulled about 60 times per like it received.

It has been revealed that the two numbers record different acts. A like states a release matters, and goes to frontier models in the weeks after they ship. A download says something is wired into a pipeline that runs on a schedule, and accrues to small, stable models over years. Likes are the right instrument for reading what the field is excited about, downloads for reading what it right now depends on. Treating either as a proxy for the other is the most common mistake we see in coverage of the Hub, including our own earlier work. The same split appears at the level of the publisher.

Recent findings suggest that china's frontier labs are the only accounts on the Hub where the heavy band carries the volume. Effectively all of MiniMax's 2026 downloads are of models above 70B, along with 88% of Moonshot's, 55% of DeepSeek's and 39% of Z.ai's. No large American account looks like this: Google, Microsoft and IBM Granite record essentially none of their 2026 downloads above 70B, and NVIDIA and Meta only 14% and 9%.

According to recent reports, the difference becomes clearer in total downloads. Moonshot’s frontier-only portfolio recorded 37M downloads over the year, while Qwen’s broader release strategy across model sizes reached 2,045M (across repositories with declared parameter counts, 2,061M including all repositories) , about 55 times more. The continued expansion of the family, from the 2.4T-parameter Qwen 3.8 Max to smaller variants such as 27B, shows the same focus on coverage across different use cases.

Time also plays an important role. Most models experience a sharp decline in usage after release, followed by a long tail of steady activity. A model’s adoption is largely determined within its first few months.

This helps explain why today’s download volume is often driven not by the newest releases, but by a smaller group of models that have become established infrastructure over time.

If frontier models were a licensing business, you would expect the biggest releases to carry the tightest terms. However, the data below reveals a different story.

Recent findings suggest that of 178 Chinese releases above 20B parameters this year, 59% carry Apache 2.0 and 22% carry MIT, and almost none carry non-commercial restrictions. However, in the last few weeks, we started to see a change on this trend for the really large models, with Kimi K3 and Qwen 3.8 2.4T starting to include some non-commercial restrictions and revenue share requirements to their licenses.

DeepSeek and Z.ai ship models between 700 billion and 1.65 trillion parameters under plain MIT. Chinese labs license their largest models about as permissively as their smallest, and more permissively than American labs license theirs: on the American side of the same size band, 29% is Apache or MIT, 41% sits under custom terms and 30% declares nothing at all.

It has been revealed that whatever these releases are for, it is not licence revenue. The weights are given away on the most permissive terms available. The return has to come from somewhere else: API and cloud business, hardware and platform positioning, or the ecosystem position itself. For instance, the valuations of Z.ai and Kimi point to an effective open source strategy, getting traction and growth opportunities in the community. Going forward, however, the industry is likely to shift toward clearer monetization paths from open-source adoption.

Industry observers note that A model’s ecosystem position is not defined only by its own releases, but by how much the community builds on top of it. As mentioned above, Qwen is one exception which is getting attention and adoption.

By this measure, Qwen has become one of the largest foundations in the open model ecosystem. Qwen-based models now account for 151,448 derivatives on the Hub, 2.6× Meta’s total footprint and 4.7× the Llama repositories specifically. Google follows with 82,506 derivatives. The third-largest source is Unsloth, a community account publishing quantized and fine-tuning-ready builds, many of which further extend the Qwen ecosystem.

In a recent development, qwen derivatives have increased at roughly 180–210 new repositories per day throughout the first seven months of 2026, showing that adoption is not driven only by individual debuts. Qwen has become part of the default workflow for developers deciding what models to fine-tune and deploy.

Several factors contributed to this position. First, consistency. Qwen has maintained a regular release cadence, continuously updating its model family rather than relying on occasional flagship releases. Second, coverage. It publishes models across a wide range of sizes and use cases, allowing developers to stay within the same ecosystem whether they need a small local model or a larger deployment model. Third, openness. Apache 2.0 licensing reduces friction for modification, redistribution, and commercial use.

These factors reinforce each other. A broad model family attracts more developers; more developers create more derivatives; and those derivatives make the ecosystem more attractive to future customers.

This position was built largely by the community. The 151,448 derivatives represent downstream work created by other developers, not releases produced by Qwen itself. Even among the 28,531 GGUF conversions of Qwen models on the Hub, Qwen published only 54.

Among models that declare a parameter count, those under 1B take 83% of all-time downloads and everything above 100B takes 1%. Restricting to downloads accumulated in 2026 changes nothing: 3% of the volume goes to models above 70B. This is the March finding that has held up most cleanly, for the same reason as before, small models are the only ones that run on the hardware most developers actually have.

Industry observers note that so how does a trillion-parameter model reach anyone at all? Through llama.cpp.

In February the ggml team joined Hugging Face, with the project remaining fully open-source, community-governed and in the same technical direction. What changed is that the most important project in local inference now has durable resources behind it.

In a recent development, the ceiling moved with llama.cpp. The July snapshot carries GGUF builds of DeepSeek-V4-Flash at roughly 284B parameters and Kimi-K3 at roughly 2.8 trillion. Local inference used to mean an 8B model on a laptop. It now means a trillion-parameter mixture-of-experts spread across a few consumer machines, which is the alternative route the frontier did not have a year ago, and the reason a frontier-first release strategy is viable at all.

In a recent development, and that route runs on Qwen: 39.6 million GGUF downloads a month, nearly twice Gemma's 20.8 million and more than five times Llama's 7.5 million. The Llama gap is not a supply problem, Llama-derived GGUF repositories slightly outnumber Qwen's. Same shelf space, a fifth of the traffic.

Sources indicate that model repositories grew 21.5% over these seven months. Several things around them grew several times faster.

Recent findings suggest that repositories declaring the gguf library rose 464%, lerobot 194% and Apple's mlx148%, against 16% for transformers and peft and 21% for diffusers. The modelling core is growing at roughly the platform average. The layer that decides where a model can physically run local inference formats, Apple silicon, robot control stacks, is growing three to seven times faster than that.

Across the ten largest model families, the labs behind these models publish very few official GGUF conversions. Yet GGUF versions are often the ones used by developers running models locally. Providing an official conversion at release, documenting quantization choices, and signing the artifacts would require limited additional effort. Rather than maintaining this workflow internally, labs could collaborate with existing ecosystem contributors such as Unsloth. Doing so would narrow the gap between the weights tested by model creators and the versions adopted by the broader community.

It has been revealed that we could not have written this section in March, because the instrument did not exist. The agent-usage dataset, published in July, records the agent/ token that coding agents send when they call the Hub through huggingface_hub or the hf CLI — searching for models, pushing datasets, running Jobs, creating Spaces. For the first time we can see how much agent traffic the Hub receives and which harnesses it comes from.

Claude Code led July with 44.4%, but a single month conceals the real finding: it held 67.8% in April and 64% in May, while Codex climbed steadily from 10.4% to 20.8%. This is a market with no incumbent, where one release or one changed default can move half the traffic in a month.

The second finding is the unregistered row. Nearly a quarter of agent-tagged traffic in July came from harnesses not yet named in the dataset, and in May that figure was 59.8%. Between April and July more than a dozen newly introduced client identifiers appeared. New entrants are arriving faster than any registry can name them — which is itself the finding.

Sources indicate that we spent much of the year building for this reader rather than only for human browsers. Papers began serving machine-readable Markdown in March. April brought agent traces as a first-class dataset type and an agents.md endpoint on every Gradio Space, so an agent can read a Space's API and call it directly. July brought the hf_fs tool on our MCP server, exposing repositories, storage, docs and papers through a single interface in just over a thousand tokens, alongside attachable sandboxes for secure execution. The same consolidation happened at the protocol layer, with MCP moving into the Linux Foundation's Agentic AI Foundation.

Then, in July, an agent stopped being a reader and became an intruder. What appears to be the first documented case of an autonomous agent running a sustained intrusion on its own initiative happened to us. While our team tried to use frontier closed models to analyze the captured attack code, their safety guardrails declined the work. The analysis was completed in the end on a quantized open model GLM-5.2 running on our own infrastructure. We published a disclosure and a full technical timeline.

Recent findings suggest that compared to the spring report, the geographical rebalancing of power continues to accelerate. While U.S. open source models continue to be competitive, the race between several Chinese frontier model labs draws strong attention. Many likes on these frontier models point to what excites the community the most, and growth opportunity for companies leveraging the attention for valuations.

In a recent development, however, the AI race is not only sprints, but also a marathon; tools like llama.cpp helps deploying the significant models locally, but a broad model family and its adoption is still the key, to build a positive feedback loop between developers, publisher and future customers. Models to be embedded in the infrastructure and being part of the ecosystem, may lead to a commercially sound exit at the end of the tunnel.

In the end, with agents being the number 1 user on HF Hub for the first time, the next report may look very different.

In AI, a few months can reshape the ecosystem.

This analysis is based on activity observed on the Hugging Face Hub during the first seven months of 2026.

Recent findings suggest that the metrics used in this report, including downloads, likes, derivatives, and model releases, represent different aspects of ecosystem activity. They should not be interpreted as direct measures of model quality, commercial adoption, or overall market share.

Downloads indicate usage within the Hub ecosystem, but they do not capture API usage, private deployments, or models distributed through other channels.

Likes reflect community attention and interest, while derivative models provide a signal of how much developers build on top of an existing model.

Because open-source AI adoption happens across many channels, Hub activity should be viewed as one perspective on ecosystem development rather than a complete measurement of the AI market.

This article was edited to include latest releases in early August.

LLMs as Validators for Cross-Chain Bridges: Evaluating Source-Level and Transaction-Level Attack Detection on Solana

📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 1 min read (225 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Arxiv

⏱️ ~1 mins left to finish
📖 0% read

In a recent development, arXiv:2611.21777v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Cross-chain bridges have suffered substantial asset losses due to vulnerabilities in their on-chain programs. On Solana, missing validation checks can enable exploits even when the underlying blockchain operates correctly. The ability of large language models (LLMs) to diagnose these flaws from source code or transaction records, rather than merely raise alarms, remains insufficiently understood. We implement a native Rust lock-and-mint bridge on a local Solana validator with four exploitable variants: two model flaws from the Cashio and Wormhole incidents, while the other two represent vulnerability classes documented in Solana security audits. Paired vulnerable and secure programs, together with successful attacks, benign sessions, and blocked attempts, allow us to distinguish correct diagnoses from unsupported alarms. We evaluate six configurations of five open-weight models across 16,800 responses, compare source inputs with and without comments, and grade 7,200 answers on vulnerable inputs using two blinded LLM graders. The results reveal substantial differences across conditions: without comments, models diagnose 24% of vulnerable source inputs while frequently flagging the secure bridge. Transaction diagnosis is high for the missing-signer scenario but averages 6% across the other three scenarios. Original comments, some of which describe the flaw, increase source diagnosis to 60%. These findings highlight the importance of distinguishing correct vulnerability diagnoses from unsupported alarms in bridge security review.

Powering agentic cloud governance: What's latest in Organization Policy

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Even as sophisticated, new zero-day exploits continue to emerge, most cybersecurity incidents still start from the same common sources: an attacker locating and exploiting a fundamental, easily preventable cloud misconfiguration.
  • Organization Policy Service can help you secure resource configurations and set up security guardrails across your Google Cloud resource hierarchy.
  • To help platform and security teams author, audit, and scale guardrails with greater speed and simplicity, we are introducing the general availability of our Organization Policy Model Context Protocol (MCP) server and natural-language constraint authoring powered by Gemini.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The front door to AI in the workplace.

Even as sophisticated, new zero-day exploits continue to emerge, most cybersecurity incidents still start from the same common sources: an attacker locating and exploiting a fundamental, easily preventable cloud misconfiguration.

Organization Policy Service can help you secure resource configurations and set up security guardrails across your Google Cloud resource hierarchy. Using a catalog of over 100 predefined policies for many common cloud governance needs, as well as Custom Organization Policy, you can more easily set up boundaries with granular control over resources.

To help platform and security teams author, audit, and scale guardrails with greater speed and simplicity, we are introducing the general availability of our Organization Policy Model Context Protocol (MCP) server and natural-language constraint authoring powered by Gemini.

Rather than forcing administrators to manually parse complex hierarchy chains, the Organization Policy MCP server offers tools that allow autonomous agents and pipelines to interact directly with Organization Policy.

Using the Organization Policy MCP server, agents can assist administrators with posture audits, drift detection, and exemption management. Key capabilities include:.

Constraint discovery: Tools like 'ListConstraints' and 'GetCustomConstraint' allow agents to understand the specific guardrails that apply to a project, folder, or organization.

Policy evaluation: The 'GetEffectivePolicy' tool calculates the effective policy after considering hierarchy inheritance and tag-based conditions. You can use this to verify if a configuration change will be compliant.

Manage policy: 'CreatePolicy' and 'CreateCustomConstraint' allow platform teams to manage guardrails via conversational workflows.

In a recent development, for example, you can combine your preferred coding agent with the Organization Policy MCP tools to create a custom dashboard to visualize the constraints applied to an organization and identify the folders and projects in the organization that have been exempted from the policy. You can also build custom agents and skills to streamline managing Organization Policy.

Figure 1: Custom dashboard created with Organization Policy MCP tools displaying enforced constraints.

Figure 2: Visualize enforced constraints and identify exemptions with Organization Policy MCP tools.

While the Organization Policy constraint catalog provides built-in managed constraints for common use cases, each organization has its own unique architectural standards. Custom Organization Policy enables customers to express these standards as a custom constraint and enforce them across supported services.

Traditionally, administrators would write these rules in common expression language (CEL), which required a sharp understanding of Google Cloud resource schemas. Today, administrators can author custom Organization Policy in natural language through a Gemini prompt.

For example, you can prompt Gemini to require the use of agent-identity in Agent Runtime, to require that all agents deployed to Agent Runtime use an approved Agent Gateway, and to prevent owners from disabling auto-upgrades on GKE, and refine custom constraints conversationally.

To help ensure safe deployments, Gemini can also generate compliant and non-compliant test resource configurations that can help you test policy and validate in dry-run mode before enforcing the constraint.

Figure 3: Define custom constraints with a natural language prompt using Gemini.

Industry observers note that for targeted examples, the sample custom constraints library from Google Cloud Professional Services features pre-authored custom constraint samples based on CIS and PCI standards. Custom constraints are supported on a wide range of Google Cloud services including core AI and compute services including Agent Runtime, Agent Search, and Agent Studio on Gemini platform, Cloud Run, and Google Kubernetes Engine.

According to recent reports, organization Policy provides proactive cloud governance of resource configurations on Google Cloud. It lets administrators enforce critical security guardrails so engineering teams can build and deploy quickly and securely.

With a growing catalog of built-in guardrails, autonomous tools for administrators, and the ability to tailor custom constraints across  Google Cloud services, Organization Policy gives enterprises the control they need to scale safely.

Explore the Organization Policy documentation to learn more about resource governance in Google Cloud and set up your foundational guardrails.

In a recent development, arXiv:2611.21766v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Practitioners choose among LLM alignment methods largely by trial and error. We provide a theoretical foundation: each pairwise method defines a vector field on the probability simplex that governs how the model redistributes mass between preferred and dispreferred completions. Projecting onto a single preferred/dispreferred pair reduces this to a one-dimensional margin ODE with a closed-form solution. These solutions reveal that DPO margins grow without bound (logarithmically as $O(\log t)$ in the gradient-flow limit) while IPO margins converge to a finite $1/(2\tau)$; that label noise induces a qualitative phase transition in DPO (unbounded $\to$ bounded) but affects IPO only quantitatively; and that gradient concentration under asymmetric weighting governs trainability at scale. We confirm all three predictions across five model families spanning four benchmarks. The closed-form solutions also enable principled method design: we prove that adding any label smoothing $\varepsilon > 0$ to SimPO creates a finite margin attractor at $\Delta^* = \beta^{-1}\log((1-\varepsilon)/\varepsilon)$, while $\varepsilon = 0$ (standard SimPO) has no attractor. We test this across three models (8B-9B) and confirm the prediction: the theory-derived configuration (TPO-S, $\varepsilon = 0.05$) is competitive with the strongest baselines, attaining the highest mean IFEval score among the compared methods on all three, validating that the predicted finite attractor is a usable operating point rather than proposing a fresh state-of-the-art loss.

#3592. Same Cluster, 33 Points More Utilization: What Changed Was the Order

📅 17 Aug 2026 • ⏱️ 13m • 📚 Deep Dive (2675 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Hugging Face ↗ Open Full Page

Same Cluster, 33 Points More Utilization: What Changed Was the Order

📅 17 Aug 2026 | ⏱️ 13 min read (2675 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hugging Face

⏱️ ~13 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that the previous post argued that utilization, not intelligence, is where the next real constraint in enterprise AI is forming, and it closed by noting that no playbook has emerged yet for what a mature GPU Management practice looks like.
  • Recent findings suggest that we built a constraint-aware GPU allocator and benchmarked it against a FIFO scheduler across seven benchmark scenarios.
  • One note on measurement before the numbers start.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that the previous post argued that utilization, not intelligence, is where the next real constraint in enterprise AI is forming, and it closed by noting that no playbook has emerged yet for what a mature GPU Management practice looks like. This is ours.

Recent findings suggest that we built a constraint-aware GPU allocator and benchmarked it against a FIFO scheduler across seven benchmark scenarios. On identical hardware, running identical workloads, GPU utilization rose by as much as 33 percentage points, and priority-weighted output rose in every one of them, by as much as 105%. Nothing about the hardware changed. What changed was the order in which allocation decisions get made.

One note on measurement before the numbers start. Every gain below is expressed as improvement over the FIFO result on the same scenario. Utilization is reported in percentage points; value is reported as a percentage increase in priority-weighted output.

Sources indicate that "Keep the GPUs busy" is not a decision a system can execute. The decision is narrower and much harder: which GPU runs which job, in which timestep, at what priority. Formally it is one binary choice per combination of GPU, job and timestep, and the output is a grid — every GPU, across the whole scheduling horizon, with a job name in each cell or nothing at all.

Four workload types compete for that grid: training, real-time inference, batch inference, and quantization. They split into two allocation shapes, and the split is where the difficulty lives. Training, batch inference and quantization are batch-like: once started, each needs a contiguous block of GPUs held without interruption until the job finishes. Real-time inference is the opposite: elastic, driven by a demand curve that changes every timestep, growing and shrinking as traffic does.

Recent findings suggest that two incompatible shapes competing for the same hardware in the same timestep is the core problem. A second heterogeneity sits inside a single type: for the same base model, training jobs range from a few hours to several days, and from one GPU to dozens.

The comparison point throughout is a FIFO-based scheduler: real-time inference served from a fixed reservation, and every other job placed in arrival order, without regard for priority.

Under the right conditions, that is a reasonable policy. When the cluster has slack, allocation order costs nothing in utilization, everything fits regardless of sequence, so FIFO and anything more sophisticated fill the same fraction of the pool. Contention is where that ordering cost stops being invisible and starts costing capacity too. It then becomes expensive in two separate ways, and they are worth taking one at a time.

Industry observers note that the reservation. Real-time inference cannot wait for capacity; the GPUs have to be there the moment traffic needs them. A scheduler that places jobs in arrival order has no mechanism for releasing GPUs during a trough and reclaiming them before the next peak, so the only way to guarantee availability is to take each real-time application's maximum demand for the day and reserve that many GPUs for the whole day. The cost lands in every hour that is not the peak. An application needing six GPUs at midday and two at 4am holds all six for twenty-four hours, and the four idle GPUs are unavailable to any batch job for the entire day. They are not being used, and they are not free either. It is why the baseline sits near half the cluster in the two scenarios where reservation dominates: 51.6% in the mixed control and 53.6% in the training-heavy case. Roughly half a pool, with much of the idle half reserved rather than free. This cost is paid whether the cluster is contended or not — contention only makes it visible.

The ordering. Under real contention, which jobs fit at all depends on the order you place them, not just on how much capacity exists. Order is not a tiebreaker applied after the capacity question is settled. Order is a capacity decision. FIFO places each job as it arrives, without weighing what that job is worth and without checking what else still has to fit inside the horizon, so high-priority work waits behind whatever asked first and capacity gets committed in placements that later jobs cannot use.

It has been revealed that the two compound. The block held for the day's maximum real-time demand is off the table for every batch job in the queue, in every hour, and whatever remains is handed out in the order the requests happened to arrive.

It is the GPU equivalent of an airline assigning aircraft to whichever charter called first, then finding nothing left to fly the route that actually pays. And GPUs reserved all day for a peak lasting a couple of hours are the grounded aircraft from the previous piece in the most literal sense: on standby, earning nothing, unavailable to anyone else.

[Figure: side-by-side allocation grids — allocator above, FIFO below, same scenario].

It has been revealed that across five benchmark scenarios built for genuine contention, the allocator improved both axes at once. Utilization moved from a 52–85% band to a 72–88% band. Priority-weighted value rose between 24.6% and 105.1%, averaging 52%. Every scenario, both metrics, no tradeoff to explain away.

The strongest single case was a training-heavy workload on 8 GPUs: utilization went from 53.6% to 87.0%, and value more than doubled, up 105%. Thirty-three points of a fixed, already-depreciating asset, recovered by reclaiming reserved standby capacity and placing the rest in priority order. (This figure reflect a single baseline ordering.).

In a recent development, the allocator removes both behaviors. Real-time demand is treated as a curve rather than a ceiling, allocated against demand at each timestep, with batch-like work occupying the troughs, bounded by the cap on how many GPUs a real-time job may swap between consecutive timesteps. And batch-like jobs are placed by priority across the whole horizon instead of in the order they arrived. The rest of this piece is how.

It has been revealed that utilization measures occupancy: what fraction of available GPU-time is allocated to something. It carries no information about what that something is worth. One scenario pulls the two apart completely, and the gap runs in a direction that is easy to miss.

In the scale test, 30 jobs across 64 GPUs, FIFO and the allocator produced identical utilization, 44.9% each, and identical throughput, 27 of 30 jobs completed. The allocator delivered 15.9% more priority-weighted value. Every dashboard reads the same. The cluster produced materially different output.

An objective that does not price priority can fill the cluster to exactly the same level, finish exactly as many jobs, and still deliver less. The previous piece argued that occupancy is a poor read on whether a cluster is earning; this is the measured version of that claim.

Sources indicate that the alternative is not a longer list of heuristic rules. Some constraints only mean anything globally, and no local rule can express them: contiguous blocks, a budget for how much GPU churn is acceptable across the entire horizon, a guarantee that running work is never preempted. To honor those, the problem has to be written down as one thing.

Five constraints define a legal allocation:.

The objective function has two terms. Allocating a GPU to a batch-like job earns a reward equal to its priority multiplied by a time-decay weight. Failing to meet real-time demand incurs a penalty proportional to the size of the shortfall.

Sources indicate that the relative size of those weights is the entire service-level policy, expressed as one number. The real-time penalty weight is 5 to 10 times greater than the allocation weight. One unit of unmet real-time demand therefore costs what 5 to 10 GPU-timesteps of equal-priority batch work costs. The asymmetry is deliberate, and it means latency obligations are enforced inside the same optimization that places batch work, rather than by a separate autoscaler competing with the scheduler for the same GPUs.

It is also what makes the elastic treatment of real-time demand safe. The allocator can hand a GPU to batch work during a trough because underserving real-time demand later is priced so far above whatever that batch work earns — the penalty, not a static reservation, is what protects availability.

Sources indicate that the time weight decays across the horizon for a reason that only makes sense in an online system: by the next scheduling run, upcoming jobs will have arrived. Capacity used now is worth more than capacity promised later.

The formal model defines what a legal, well-scored allocation looks like. Answering an incoming request is a separate job, and it belongs to a separate component. This is NP-hard combinatorial allocation, and the scheduler is re-invoked every time a job arrives, so the decision has to come back in the gap between two API requests. That latency budget is the fixed constraint the architecture is designed around, which is why a heuristic sits on the hot path and the formal model sits behind it as the specification the heuristic is built to satisfy.

Recent findings suggest that that heuristic is not a generic greedy allocator. Its rules are the formal model's structural constraints, which means every grid it produces is a legal allocation by construction. Not usually valid. Valid by design.

According to recent reports, that design, applied across the whole horizon rather than one arrival at a time, is what produces the utilization gain. The allocator sees every queued job before it places any of them, it can hold the free pool in shapes the remaining work can actually occupy, a batch job needing a contiguous block of a given size still has room when its turn comes. Priority decides who gets first claim on that room. FIFO has neither view: it commits capacity to whichever job asked first, and a job that arrives later and needs a specific shape may find nothing left that fits, so it goes unscheduled and the GPU-hours it would have consumed go unclaimed.

It runs in 1 to 2 milliseconds on the five contended scenarios, and 15 milliseconds at 64 GPUs and 30 jobs — fast enough to run on every incoming request.

In a recent development, the system exposes two modes. Fast mode runs the allocator alone and returns its grid; this is the hot path. Full mode uses that grid as a starting point for the formal model, which attempts to improve on it — suited to periodic review rather than per-request decisions.

Utilization improved in every scenario but one, where it tied exactly. Value improved in all seven.

The scale test matters because it holds at size: 64 GPUs, 30 jobs, 15 milliseconds, 15.9% more value.

It has been revealed that the uniform-priority test matters because it addresses the obvious skeptical reading. Override every job to identical priority, so that no priority signal distinguishes any of them, and the allocator still moves utilization from 76.8% to 87.5% and value up 23.1%. The gain is not purely an artifact of ordering by priority. Planning placements across the horizon contributes on its own.

Everything above assumes the scheduler knows how many GPU-hours each job needs and how much real-time traffic is coming. Both are predictions, not inputs, and a scheduler is only as good as they are.

Recent findings suggest that A single generic estimator does not work, because the four workload types have qualitatively different cost drivers. This is where the specialization argument from the previous piece reconnects: the same logic that makes a task-specific model outperform a generalist applies to the estimators feeding the scheduler.

In a recent development, training is not one workload. It varies along two independent, freely combinable axes. Strategy determines how much of the model is updated (full fine-tuning against parameter-efficient methods like LoRA). Technique determines the optimization objective and the training loop (SFT, DPO, RLHF, RLVR, CPT). The differences are not marginal: LoRA cuts trainable parameters by up to 10,000× and GPU memory roughly 3× against full fine-tuning, on the same base model. DPO removes both the reward model and the sampling loop of RLHF. Estimating from model size alone averages across runs that differ by orders of magnitude, in exactly the two quantities the scheduler decides on, duration and GPU count. Our training forecaster conditions on 22 features, including a categorical variable distinguishing 10 concrete training variants.

In a recent development, quantization is a schedulable job, not a background chore. Quantizing a single large model can consume hours of GPU time on hardware that other work is waiting for. It gets its own forecast, built from calibration tiers by parameter count, with distinct handling per algorithm (bitsandbytes, AWQ, GPTQ) and a safety margin before rounding up to whole GPU-hours. Prior work in this area places quantization outside scheduling scope entirely.

In a recent development, real-time inference is not estimated per job at all. It is forecast as a continuously recalibrated weekly demand profile, rebuilt from hourly traffic history and mapped to GPU counts under the same swap cost the formal model enforces. Forecast and optimizer therefore agree on what churn costs, rather than disagreeing and fighting each other. This forecast is what replaces peak reservation. A per-timestep demand curve is the only thing that lets the scheduler release GPUs during a trough with any confidence that they can be reclaimed before the next peak.

This closes back to the ordering argument. Better demand estimates are what make priority-aware placement possible in the first place, you cannot sequence jobs well without knowing what they will consume.

Sources indicate that the obvious objection to all of this is that forecasts are wrong. What happens then?

According to recent reports, the failure mode to avoid has a name worth borrowing: the end-of-world effect. An optimizer that cannot see past the end of its horizon makes present decisions that wreck the timesteps immediately outside it, because as far as the model is concerned, nothing exists after the horizon ends.

The architecture answers both problems at once. The scheduler optimizes a 24-hour horizon, but commits only the current timestep, and re-runs every 30 to 60 minutes. Run at 9am, and the 9am allocation is real; the plan for 10am through 5pm exists only so that the 9am decision is made by a model that knows a future exists. The real 10am allocation comes from the 10am run, against fresh data.

The consequence is that forecast error is absorbed by re-optimization instead of compounding. Each run inherits what is actually running and pins it in place, so successive prepares enhancement rather than thrash.

There is a secondary payoff. The horizon plan is itself a forecasting product: it surfaces real-time coverage risk and predictable idle windows before they arrive, which is useful whether or not those specific allocations are ever committed.

This is also why the time-decay weight exists. By the next run, the workload mix will have changed.

Airlines did not solve utilization by computing an optimal schedule. They solved it by encoding operational discipline into the order things happen (turnaround sequence, maintenance windows, crew rostering) and letting that discipline compound.

According to recent reports, the same thing happened here. Thirty-three points of utilization in the hardest-packed scenario, and 52% more priority-weighted output on average, on the same hardware, with the same workloads, in a couple of milliseconds, came from encoding what the cluster physically permits into the order decisions get made. Structure beat sophistication.

The previous piece argued that specialization and orchestration are two halves of one problem: specialization shrinks what each workload needs, and orchestration decides where the difference goes. Neither lever pays off alone. This is what the second half looks like when it is built.

Industry observers note that the GPUs were already installed, already committed, already depreciating. The gain was in how we chose to spend them.

From Top to Bottom: Quark Mass Hierarchies in Heterotic String Theory

📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 1 min read (201 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Arxiv

⏱️ ~1 mins left to finish
📖 0% read

arXiv:2611.21751v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Standard Model fermion masses exhibit large hierarchies, spanning more than five orders of magnitude in the quark sector alone. In this paper, we study whether these hierarchies can be generated perturbatively at tree level in smooth heterotic Calabi-Yau compactifications, where the supergravity approximation remains under computational control. In such backgrounds, physical Yukawa couplings combine holomorphic superpotential integrals with matter field Kahler metrics. The former can be computed algebraically, while the latter require solving a coupled system of partial differential equations for the Ricci-flat metric, Hermitian Yang-Mills connections, and harmonic bundle-valued forms. Within this framework, we identify two new tree-level mechanisms by which complex structure moduli can generate fermion mass hierarchies and show analytically and numerically that both mechanisms are obstructed for previously studied tetra-quadric models. Motivated by these obstructions, we scan the existing databases of tens of thousands of complete intersection Calabi-Yau line bundle models and find a unique smooth quotient admitting a rank-three up-quark Yukawa matrix at tree level. Evaluating the physical couplings on this manifold and evolving them under the renormalization group, we obtain realistic mass hierarchies for the top, charm, up, and bottom quarks in the smooth supergravity regime.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Healthcare Lead, Chrome Enterprise Ecosystem, Google.

Chrome Enterprise Premium offers enhanced protections for patient data.

Recent findings suggest that healthcare is adopting AI promptly, and it's moving beyond chat. Clinical teams are starting to use AI agents that draft documentation, summarize charts, navigate web apps, and complete multi-step tasks on a clinician's behalf. Many of these agents work in the same place—the browser. As electronic health records (EHRs) and clinical apps move to the web, the browser is where clinicians, applications, patient data, and AI services meet. When clinicians or agents act inside a session, security teams need clear control over what they can access.

Sources indicate that healthcare systems frequently adopt a multi-vendor AI strategy, a flexibility that should be fully supported. Whether clinicians are using Gemini™ or an array of other web-based AI tools and extensions, Chrome Enterprise Premium secures data across the board to:.

Industry observers note that since we introduced new healthcare integrations in May, Chrome Enterprise has continued to invest in the healthcare ecosystem. Today we're sharing the next set of milestones that bring Chrome Enterprise to more clinical endpoints.

Chrome Enterprise is now compatible with IGEL OS™.

As healthcare organizations accelerate the adoption of web-based clinical applications and AI-powered workflows, securing both the browser and the endpoint has become increasingly important. To address this, Chrome Enterprise is now compatible with the IGEL Adaptive Secure Endpoint Platform™ and will soon be available in the IGEL App Portal,® allowing healthcare IT teams to easily deploy and manage the browser across IGEL OS™ endpoints, including shared workstations, nursing stations, and clinical carts.

According to recent reports, this collaboration combines Google's enterprise-grade browser management and security capabilities with the IGEL Adaptive Secure Endpoint Platform,™ providing an immutable, trusted, and centrally governed endpoint foundation designed to reduce the attack surface and simplify IT operations. Through the IGEL App Portal® and IGEL Universal Management Suite™ (UMS™), organizations can streamline application deployment and endpoint governance, while the Google Admin console provides centralized browser policy and extension management.

Native browsing for flexible clinical endpoints with Citrix® UniconOS.

Sources indicate that through our expanded collaboration with Citrix, healthcare systems can now run Chrome Enterprise natively on Citrix UniconOS endpoints. Clinicians get a fast, familiar experience on any device, while IT gains another flexible option for adding secure access and data protections across their clinical environments.

Expanding collaboration with Omnissa® for enhanced device trust.

Many healthcare organizations use Omnissa Workspace ONE® and Omnissa Horizon® to manage, secure and deliver critical clinical applications. We're expanding our collaboration with Omnissa to bring zero-trust security and device posture assessment to healthcare environments. Building on May's integration, organizations can verify device health before clinicians reach critical applications.

Optimizing Epic® Workflows at the point of care.

Beyond endpoint expansion, we are introducing new Chrome Enterprise capabilities that streamline clinic workflows, including support for silent printing and PDF updates for Epic® Hyperspace® for the web. This allows clinicians to route essential orders and wristbands directly to authorized printers, while native PDF rendering keeps protected health information strictly isolated within the active, managed session.

Scaling clinical technology with confidence.

Together, these updates give IT and security teams the confidence to say yes to modern clinical technology, supporting the patient care experience—without giving up critical protections and control. As healthcare organizations continue deploying enterprise AI solutions like Gemini or managing a fast-growing ecosystem of third-party AI web apps and browser extensions, Chrome Enterprise provides the unified security, Data Loss Prevention (DLP), and governance layer needed to empower care teams with confidence.

To get started, explore Chrome Enterprise in the IGEL Marketplace, see how our latest updates support your Epic® and clinical workflows or visit our website or contact us today.

arXiv:2611.21707v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: We introduce EJBench, a benchmark of engineering judgement: whether a model can predict how a design behaves at newly introduced conditions from a few earlier results, and decide on it. Unlike engineering benchmarks that test whether an agent can operate simulation or CAD software, EJBench is software-agnostic and asks what an engineer would conclude without running a simulation. Its tasks come from a conjugate heat transfer design campaign for battery cold plates, in three families: matching unlabelled test results to their operating points, choosing which stored runs to reveal before signing off a design, and ranking new duties by peak cell temperature. Every answer is taken from a converged simulation, not from an LLM judge. The best of ten frontier models, GPT-6 Astra, scores 0.71, and models state almost the same confidence on tasks they get wrong as on tasks they get right. We also post-train Qwen3.5-9B with LoRA and reinforcement learning, rewarded by the share of answer criteria the simulation results confirm; on the held-out test split its score rises from 0.071 to 0.106. We release the train, validation and test splits, the evaluation harness and the leaderboard.
